newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: FEATURE - Bangladesh hilltribes fight for rights.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Bangladesh hilltribes fight for rights.

text.p: The 23-year separatist insurgency in Bangladesh's southeastern Chittagong Hill Tracts seems to have its roots in fears that the area's tribespeople may be overrun by outsiders, military and civil officials said.
They said such fears give the rebel Shanti Bahini (peace force) a platform for its armed campaign for political autonomy for the 5,500 sq-mile (14,200 sq-km) Hill Tracts bordering India and Burma.
Bangladesh has deployed about 30,000 security personnel to deal with an estimated 3,000 Shanti Bahini guerrillas, alleged to be trained in India.

"We can crush the insurgency should that be the policy of the government. But it sincerely wants a political settlement in the Hill Tracts through negotiations," Brigadier A.T.M. Zahirul Alam, counter-insurgency commander in Rangamati, told Reuters.

The insurgency and battles between tribespeople and Moslem settlers have together killed more than 8,500 people since the Shantis took up arms in 1973 after Bangladesh rejected their demand for autonomy, officials said.
The victims include some 500 security men, 5,000 settlers and 3,000 tribals who were seeking to drive the settlers away.
The settlers moved to the Hill Tracts in the early 1980s under a government plan, and are often accused of stealing tribal land and destroying their culture.
But what disturbs the tribespeople most is the fear that they might be outnumbered by Moslems and overwhelmed, tribal leaders said.

"Fear rules the minds of our people," said Suniti Bikash Chakma, a tribal leader. "The problem of the Hill Tracts is an ethnic problem, which has not been properly identified by the government," he told Reuters.

He said that former Bangladesh president Hossain Mohammad Ershad had created Local Government Councils in three Hill Tracts districts in 1989 and promised to give them a range of powers, including control of police, local taxes and education.
"But those bodies have become virtually redundant because the powers have not been delegated and no council election has been held since Ershad lost power in 1990."
Other tribal leaders blamed the insurgency largely on what they said was a lack of constitutional guarantees for the rights of the tribespeople.
"The tribals and non-tribals are always ready for a fight. The settlers are taking control of tribal land, often by force," said Shantimoy Chakma, a teacher.
Promises that tribal land occupied by settlers would be returned have seldom been honoured, said Subinoy Chakma, another member of the Chakma tribe.
The Chakmas are the largest among 13 tribes, representing nearly 60 percent of Chittagong Hill Tracts' population, and are also the main supporters of the Shanti Bahini.

Subinoy said a group of Chakmas, including himself, Moslems and Hindus had some years ago set up a committee to advise the government on ending the tribal insurgency, which has forced thousands of tribal families to flee to northeast India.
"But the job is not easy. It appears that neither the authorities nor the rebels believe us," he said.
"The Shantis call us dalals (agents) of the government. The government suspects we work for the Shantis. We are often threatened...," he added.
Brigadier Alam said he believed the Shanti Bahini guerrillas were misled by their leaders, who had a strong political past and are now hiding across the border.
"Ordinary tribespeople and even a section of the guerrillas seem to have realised that they are chasing a mirage."
"But it is hard for them to escape the influence of their leaders," he said without elaborating.

Alam said the tribespeople in the Hill Tracts were well placed economically, in education and employment, and were enjoying special privileges granted to them as part of the government's peace intitiatives.

"The tribals have been given ownership of rubber gardens, they have a 50 percent job quota in development projects. There are no beggars among them, and the tribespeople still keep their own feudal system while enjoying benefits of democratic administration," he said .
"But their own Shanti Bahini threaten them, burn down rubber plants and scare them away from jobs. That's not the fault of the government," Alam said.
The tribals disagree. "There has been a lack of goodwill on both sides. And there is a strong need for proper policy to stop acrimony between local and outsiders," Shantimoy said.
